description: Citation universe for the linux-tut course. Every fact-about-the-world in the course (defaults, guarantees, numbers, incidents, quotes) must trace to one of these primary sources, verified by fetching the actual source. Each entry lists claims the course intends to make; the verification agent must mark each confirmed / corrected / unverifiable against the fetched text, with quote and location. 'group' assigns the source to a research agent. Verification agents may add sources in their group if a planned claim is better supported elsewhere (primary sources only).

claims.finding: what the source actually says, precisely, with numbers
claims.cite_url: deep link if different from canonical

extra_findings: verified facts not planned but useful to the course, each with quote+location
note_format.teaching_notes: what this source uniquely offers; folklore it contradicts

sources.title: GNU Bash Reference Manual
planned_claims: Exit status: 0 is success, non-zero failure; range 0-255; command not found returns 127; found but not executable returns 126; a command terminated by fatal signal N returns 128+N
Pipeline exit status is that of the last command unless pipefail is set; with pipefail it is the last (rightmost) command to exit non-zero
set -e (errexit) semantics and its documented exceptions (conditions in if/while, && || lists, non-final pipeline commands, negated commands)
set -u (nounset) treats unset variables as an error on expansion
Redirection semantics: order matters, `>file 2>&1` vs `2>&1 >file`; `&>` shorthand; here-documents and here-strings; /dev/fd, /dev/tcp special filenames
Quoting: single quotes preserve literally; double quotes preserve all but $ ` \ (and ! with history); word splitting and filename expansion happen on unquoted expansions
Builtins such as cd, export, source exist because they must change the shell's own state

Startup files: login vs interactive non-login vs non-interactive shells (which of /etc/profile, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bashrc, BASH_ENV are read) — matters because harness `bash -c` shells read none of the interactive ones
Command search order: functions, builtins, then PATH lookup; hash table

sources.title: POSIX.1-2017/2024 Shell Command Language & Utilities (The Open Group Base Specifications)
planned_claims: POSIX specifies exit status 127 for command not found and 126 for found-but-not-executable, and >128 for signal termination
Standard streams: stdin 0, stdout 1, stderr 2
sh is the portable shell language; bash features (arrays, [[ ]], pipefail historically) are extensions — check whether pipefail was added in POSIX.1-2024

sources.title: GNU Coreutils manual
planned_claims: timeout: sends TERM by default; exit status 124 on timeout; 125 if timeout itself fails; 126/127 for not-executable/not-found; 137 when KILL is sent (-k / -s KILL) ; --kill-after behaviour; --preserve-status
uniq only collapses ADJACENT duplicate lines, hence sort | uniq
sort is locale-dependent; LC_ALL=C gives byte ordering (reproducibility point)
rm: -r, -f semantics; --preserve-root is default (rm -rf / refused)
ls -l output fields; chmod symbolic and numeric modes; chown syntax; mktemp; tee; head/tail -f; wc; cut; tr; env; nohup; stat; df/du; readlink/realpath

sources.title: ShellCheck wiki / README
planned_claims: ShellCheck is a static analysis tool for sh/bash scripts
SC2086 (double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting) wording; SC2164 (cd … || exit); SC2046; SC2155

sources.title: jq Manual
planned_claims: jq processes a stream of JSON values, so it reads JSONL (one object per line) natively; -c compact output; -r raw strings; -s slurp; select(), group_by, length; exit status with -e

sources.title: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard 3.0
planned_claims: Purpose of /bin /sbin /etc /home /root /var /var/log /tmp /usr /usr/local /opt /proc /sys /dev /run /srv /mnt /media as specified
/tmp contents need not persist between boots / program invocations; /var/tmp is preserved between reboots
/etc holds host-specific configuration; /var holds variable data; /usr is shareable read-only data

sources.title: hier(7) and file-hierarchy(7)
planned_claims: Linux-specific descriptions of the tree incl. /run, /proc, /sys; /usr merge (bin -> usr/bin symlinks) on modern distros

sources.title: inode(7), link(2), symlink(7), path_resolution(7)
planned_claims: An inode holds file metadata (type, mode, owner uid/gid, size, timestamps, link count) but NOT the filename; names live in directories
Hard link = another name for the same inode; file data is freed when link count reaches 0 AND no process has it open (unlink(2)) — explains 'deleted but still using disk'
Symlink permissions are ignored / always 0777; permission of the target applies; dangling symlinks
path_resolution: search (execute) permission needed on every directory in the path

sources.title: credentials(7), passwd(5), shadow(5), group(5)
planned_claims: Processes carry real, effective, saved UIDs/GIDs and supplementary groups; the kernel checks numeric IDs, names are just a lookup in /etc/passwd
UID 0 is the superuser; privilege is tied to effective UID 0 (traditionally) and to capabilities
/etc/passwd format: seven colon-separated fields (name:password:UID:GID:GECOS:directory:shell); world-readable; password field 'x' means hash is in /etc/shadow
/etc/shadow readable only by root (and shadow group); fields
A child process inherits its parent's credentials

sources.title: chmod(2), chmod(1), umask(2), chown(2), sticky/setuid semantics
planned_claims: Mode bits and octal values: S_ISUID 04000, S_ISGID 02000, S_ISVTX 01000, rwx for user/group/other 0400..0001

Permission check uses exactly ONE class: owner if UID matches, else group if a GID matches, else other (so owner with 0 perms is denied even if 'other' allows) — find authoritative wording (path_resolution(7) or inode(7) or POSIX)
Directory bits: r = list names, w = create/delete entries, x = search/traverse; deleting a file needs write on the DIRECTORY, not the file
Sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion to file owner, directory owner, or privileged process (why /tmp is 1777)
umask clears bits from the mode requested at creation: files typically created 0666 & ~umask, dirs 0777 & ~umask; common default 022
Only a privileged process (CAP_CHOWN) may change a file's owner; owner may change group to one they belong to
Set-user-ID: execve sets effective UID to file owner; ignored for scripts on Linux; ignored under nosuid mounts and no_new_privs
Root (CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE) bypasses read/write/execute permission checks (execute only if some x bit is set) — cite capabilities(7)

sources.title: sudo(8) / sudoers(5) manual
planned_claims: sudo executes a command as another user (default root) according to the sudoers policy; NOPASSWD tag; sudo -l lists what the invoking user may run; env_reset default resets environment
Official minimal images (ubuntu, debian) do not ship sudo — verify by running, not from docs

sources.title: signal(7), kill(2), kill(1)
planned_claims: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored
Signal numbers on x86/ARM: HUP 1, INT 2, QUIT 3, KILL 9, SEGV 11, PIPE 13, ALRM 14, TERM 15, CHLD 17, CONT 18, STOP 19, TSTP 20; default dispositions (Term/Core/Ign/Stop)
kill(1) sends TERM by default; kill -0 tests existence/permission; negative PID signals a process group
Permission to signal: sender needs CAP_KILL or matching real/effective UID
SIGPIPE is sent when writing to a pipe with no reader (explains `yes | head`)

sources.title: PID 1 semantics: pid_namespaces(7); Docker --init / tini
planned_claims: In a PID namespace the first process is PID 1 ('init'); orphans are reparented to it; if it terminates the kernel SIGKILLs all other processes in the namespace

Signals for which PID 1 has not installed a handler are not delivered to it from inside the namespace (so an app running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM unless it handles it); from the parent namespace only SIGKILL/SIGSTOP are forced
docker run --init runs an init (tini) as PID 1 that forwards signals and reaps zombies
docker stop sends SIGTERM (or STOPSIGNAL) then SIGKILL after a grace period, default 10 seconds

sources.title: fork(2), execve(2), wait(2), exit(3), environ(7)
planned_claims: fork creates a child that is a copy of the parent incl. open file descriptors and environment; execve replaces the program image, keeping PID, open fds (unless close-on-exec), and the environment passed to it
A terminated child remains a zombie until the parent wait()s; zombies hold a PID/table slot but no memory; orphans are adopted by init (or nearest subreaper)
Only the low 8 bits of the exit status are available to the parent (status & 0xFF) — hence 0-255
environ: array of name=value strings, inherited by children via exec; by convention uppercase; a child cannot change its parent's environment

sources.title: proc(5) and its sub-pages (proc_pid_environ, proc_pid_status, proc_pid_fd, proc_pid_cmdline, proc_meminfo, proc_loadavg)
planned_claims: /proc is a pseudo-filesystem exposing kernel data structures; /proc/PID/ directories per process
/proc/PID/environ holds the INITIAL environment set at exec, NUL-separated; readable subject to ptrace access mode check (same user or root)
/proc/PID/cmdline is world-readable by default → secrets passed as command-line arguments are visible to every user via ps; hidepid mount option can restrict
/proc/PID/fd is a directory of symlinks to open files; /proc/PID/cwd, /proc/PID/exe, /proc/PID/status fields (Uid, Gid, VmRSS, CapEff, NoNewPrivs, Seccomp)
/proc/loadavg: 1, 5, 15 minute load averages count runnable AND uninterruptible (D state) tasks
/proc/meminfo MemAvailable definition vs MemFree

sources.title: getrlimit(2)/setrlimit(2), bash ulimit
planned_claims: Resource limits have soft and hard values; unprivileged process can lower hard limit irreversibly and raise soft up to hard; inherited across fork, preserved across exec
RLIMIT_NOFILE, RLIMIT_NPROC (per real UID, not per process tree), RLIMIT_AS, RLIMIT_CPU (SIGXCPU then SIGKILL), RLIMIT_FSIZE (SIGXFSZ), RLIMIT_CORE
rlimits are per-process, unlike cgroup limits which apply to a group — contrast for page 12/21

sources.title: Kernel docs: cgroup v2 memory controller & OOM; Docker resource constraints
planned_claims: memory.max is a hard limit; if usage reaches it and cannot be reclaimed, the OOM killer is invoked in the cgroup
memory.events has oom and oom_kill counters — the authoritative way to tell that a container's process was OOM-killed; memory.current, memory.peak, memory.high (throttle), memory.swap.max
OOM-killed process receives SIGKILL → exit status 137 seen by shell/Docker; docker inspect State.OOMKilled field
Docker: by default a container has no resource constraints; -m/--memory, --memory-swap semantics (if --memory set and --memory-swap unset, swap = same amount again → total 2x), --cpus, --pids-limit
cpu.max format 'quota period' (e.g. '150000 100000' = 1.5 CPUs); CPU limit throttles rather than kills; cpu.stat nr_throttled/throttled_usec
pids.max limits number of processes; fork fails with EAGAIN when reached (fork-bomb containment)
cgroup v2 single unified hierarchy mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup; a process belongs to exactly one cgroup; /proc/PID/cgroup shows it; controllers listed in cgroup.controllers

sources.title: systemd documentation: systemd(1), systemctl(1), journalctl(1), systemd.service(5), systemd-journald
planned_claims: systemd is the system and service manager running as PID 1 on most mainstream distros; units (service, socket, timer, mount, target); unit file search paths /etc/systemd/system overrides /usr/lib/systemd/system
systemctl status/start/stop/enable/disable/list-units --type=service / --failed; enable ≠ start

journald collects stdout/stderr of services, syslog, kernel messages; journalctl -u UNIT, -b, -f, -p err, --since, -k; storage volatile (/run/log/journal) vs persistent (/var/log/journal) per Storage= setting
Stopping a service: KillMode=control-group default, SIGTERM then SIGKILL after TimeoutStopSec (default 90s)
Restart= policies; services run in their own cgroup (systemd-cgls)
Typical Docker containers do NOT run systemd; PID 1 is the app, logs go to container stdout/stderr → docker logs (cite Docker docs for logging: json-file default driver)

sources.title: procps-ng: ps(1), top(1), free(1), uptime(1), pgrep/pkill
planned_claims: ps process state codes: R running/runnable, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep, Z zombie, T stopped; ps aux vs ps -ef columns (RSS in KiB, VSZ, STAT, TTY '?')
free: 'available' column is the estimate of memory available for new applications, not 'free'; buff/cache is reclaimable
top summary fields: load average, us/sy/id/wa/st CPU states

sources.title: strace(1); syscalls(2) intro
planned_claims: A system call is the fundamental interface between an application and the Linux kernel; strace traces system calls and signals; -f follows forks; -e trace=… filters; requires ptrace permission (blocked by default Docker seccomp? verify: Docker default seccomp allows ptrace on kernels ≥4.8)

sources.title: namespaces(7) and per-type pages: mount_namespaces(7), network_namespaces(7), user_namespaces(7), uts_namespaces(7), ipc_namespaces(7), cgroup_namespaces(7), time_namespaces(7); unshare(1), nsenter(1), lsns(8)
planned_claims: Definition: a namespace wraps a global system resource in an abstraction that makes it appear to processes within it that they have their own isolated instance; one use is to implement containers
The namespace types and what each isolates (cgroup, IPC, network, mount, PID, time, user, UTS) — exact table
/proc/PID/ns/* symlinks identify namespaces; two processes are in the same namespace iff the inode numbers match
A new network namespace has only a loopback interface (down); a physical device lives in exactly one netns; veth pairs connect namespaces

User namespaces: UID/GID mappings (uid_map), a process can be root (UID 0, full capabilities) INSIDE a user namespace while unprivileged outside; capabilities in a user ns only govern resources owned by that ns
Creating namespaces other than user requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN

There is no kernel object called a 'container': a container is a userspace convention combining namespaces + cgroups + a root filesystem + security restrictions (find best authoritative wording — namespaces(7) 'one use of namespaces is to implement containers'; possibly OCI runtime-spec)
The kernel itself is NOT namespaced/shared: all containers on a host share one kernel (uname -r identical) — supports the 'shared kernel' argument of page 24

sources.title: cgroups(7)
planned_claims: Definition: control groups allow processes to be organized into hierarchical groups whose usage of resources can be limited and monitored; interface is a pseudo-filesystem (cgroupfs)
cgroups v1 vs v2: v2 unified hierarchy; controllers available in v2 (cpu, memory, io, pids, cpuset, …)
Namespaces control what a process can SEE; cgroups control how much it can USE (teaching framing — mark as framing, but confirm the two definitions support it)

sources.title: capabilities(7)
planned_claims: Linux divides the privileges traditionally associated with superuser into distinct units (capabilities) that can be independently enabled/disabled, per-thread
CAP_SYS_ADMIN is overloaded ('the new root'), includes mount(2), etc. — exact man page wording

What these allow: CAP_NET_RAW (raw sockets → ping, packet sniffing), CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE (ports <1024), CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, CAP_CHOWN, CAP_KILL, CAP_SETUID, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, CAP_SYS_MODULE, CAP_SYS_CHROOT, CAP_MKNOD
Capability sets: permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding, ambient; /proc/PID/status CapEff etc; capsh --decode / getpcaps

sources.title: seccomp(2); kernel docs: seccomp_filter, no_new_privs; Docker seccomp profile docs
planned_claims: seccomp filter mode lets a process install a BPF filter restricting which system calls it (and its children) may make; reduces kernel attack surface; kernel docs say it is 'not a sandbox' by itself
no_new_privs: once set, execve cannot grant privileges (setuid/setgid bits and file capabilities have no effect); inherited, cannot be unset

Docker's default seccomp profile is an allowlist that 'disables around 44 system calls out of 300+' — verify the current number and wording; examples of blocked calls (mount, reboot, kexec_load, init_module, keyctl…)
--security-opt seccomp=unconfined disables; --privileged disables seccomp

sources.title: Docker AppArmor security profiles
planned_claims: Docker auto-generates and loads a default profile 'docker-default' for containers on AppArmor-enabled hosts; it is 'moderately protective'

sources.title: mount(8), findmnt(8), mount(2), tmpfs(5), proc_pid_mountinfo(5), chroot(2), pivot_root(2)
planned_claims: All files are arranged in one big tree rooted at /; mount attaches a filesystem found on some device to the tree

Mount options: ro, rw, nosuid, nodev, noexec; remount; bind mounts (mount --bind) and that a read-only bind requires remount,bind,ro (historical) or works directly on newer util-linux — get exact current wording

tmpfs lives in virtual memory (RAM+swap), contents lost on unmount; size= option, default half of RAM; counts toward the memory cgroup of the writer? (verify in kernel cgroup-v2 doc: shmem/tmpfs charged to memory cgroup)
chroot changes the root directory of the calling process; it is NOT intended as a security mechanism / to sandbox a process — exact man page wording; pivot_root is what container runtimes use
/proc/self/mountinfo is the kernel's authoritative list; findmnt renders it as a tree; findmnt -T path, findmnt -O ro

sources.title: Kernel docs: Overlay Filesystem; Docker overlay2/ storage driver docs (or containerd image store)
planned_claims: Overlayfs merges an upper (writable) and one or more lower (read-only) directory trees; modifications go to upper; first write to a lower file triggers copy-up of the whole file; deletions recorded as whiteouts
Docker images are stacks of read-only layers; a container adds a thin writable layer on top; writable-layer data is deleted with the container; containers from the same image share the lower layers

Deleting a file in a later layer does NOT remove it from the image: it remains in the earlier layer and can be extracted (critical for solution leakage / secrets in images) — find Docker docs wording (Dockerfile best practices / build secrets docs)
Current default storage in Docker Engine 28/29: overlay2 vs containerd image store (verify what is default for fresh installs)

sources.title: RFC 1918 Address Allocation for Private Internets; RFC 4632 CIDR; RFC 6890/5735 special-purpose (127/8, 169.254/16); RFC 6598 (100.64/10)
planned_claims: CIDR prefix notation: /n = n leading network bits; a /24 has 256 addresses

sources.title: Cloud instance metadata service docs (AWS IMDS; GCP metadata server)
planned_claims: Instance metadata is served at link-local 169.254.169.254 and can include temporary IAM role credentials → a sandboxed agent on a cloud VM with open egress to that address can read the host's cloud credentials; IMDSv2 requires a session token (PUT) and has a hop limit (default 1) that blocks containers one hop away — verify exact defaults

sources.title: iproute2: ip(8), ip-address(8), ip-route(8), ip-link(8), ss(8), veth(4)
planned_claims: ip addr / ip route / ip link usage and output fields; `ip route get ADDR` shows the route the kernel would use; default route = 'default via GW dev IF'
ss -tulpn flags meaning (tcp, udp, listening, processes, numeric); State/Local Address:Port columns; process column requires privilege for others' sockets
veth devices are created in pairs; packets sent on one are received on the other; used to connect network namespaces
ip(7): ports below 1024 are privileged (need CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE) subject to net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start; INADDR_ANY (0.0.0.0) binds all interfaces; INADDR_LOOPBACK
net-tools (ifconfig, netstat, route) is deprecated/unmaintained in favour of iproute2 — find a primary statement (Debian wiki / net-tools page) or mark unverifiable

sources.title: tcp(7), udp(7), RFC 9293 (TCP), RFC 768 (UDP), RFC 6335 (port ranges)
planned_claims: TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-oriented byte stream; UDP: connectionless, unreliable datagrams
Port ranges: System 0-1023, User 1024-49151, Dynamic/Private 49152-65535 (RFC 6335); Linux ephemeral default range from ip_local_port_range 32768-60999

Connection refused = RST from a reachable host with no listener; timeout = packets dropped (firewall DROP or no route) — find authoritative support (RFC 9293 reset generation; connect(2) ECONNREFUSED/ETIMEDOUT)

sources.title: resolv.conf(5), hosts(5), nsswitch.conf(5), dig(1) (BIND 9 docs), RFC 1034/1035, systemd-resolved
planned_claims: resolv.conf: nameserver (max 3), search, options ndots; nsswitch 'hosts: files dns' order means /etc/hosts wins before DNS

dig output sections (QUESTION, ANSWER, status NOERROR/NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL, SERVER line); dig +short; dig bypasses nsswitch//etc/hosts (queries DNS directly) while getent hosts uses the system resolver path
DNS uses UDP and TCP port 53; record types A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS
Ubuntu uses systemd-resolved stub at 127.0.0.53
Docker: containers on user-defined networks use embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11; default bridge copies host resolv.conf; containers resolve each other by name only on user-defined networks

DNS as an egress channel: DNS queries leave the sandbox even when HTTP is blocked unless resolver access is also controlled (framing; look for a primary source on DNS tunnelling/exfiltration e.g. MITRE ATT&CK T1071.004)

sources.title: curl man page / Everything curl
planned_claims: curl -v shows connection, TLS handshake, request (>) and response (<) headers; -s -S -f -L -o -I -m/--max-time --connect-timeout; -f makes HTTP errors (≥400) return exit 22
curl exit codes: 6 couldn't resolve host, 7 failed to connect, 28 operation timeout, 35 SSL connect error, 60 peer certificate cannot be authenticated — perfect mapping from symptom to network layer
Proxy environment variables: http_proxy (lowercase only for http), HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY honoured by curl
--cacert / -k(--insecure) semantics; CA bundle

sources.title: TLS 1.3 RFC 8446 (intro only); HTTP semantics RFC 9110 (status code classes); ca-certificates package; update-ca-certificates(8)
planned_claims: TLS goals: authentication (server always, via certificate), confidentiality, integrity (RFC 8446 §1)
HTTP status classes 1xx–5xx; methods GET/POST; 407 Proxy Authentication Required; 403 vs 404

System trust store on Debian/Ubuntu: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt built by update-ca-certificates from /usr/local/share/ca-certificates; minimal images lack the ca-certificates package so HTTPS fails with a certificate error until installed (verify by running)
A TLS-intercepting egress proxy requires its CA to be installed in the sandbox trust store; SNI is visible in cleartext enabling hostname allowlists without decryption (RFC 8446 / RFC 6066)

sources.title: nftables wiki, nft(8), iptables(8), Docker packet filtering docs
planned_claims: nftables replaces iptables/ip6tables/arptables/ebtables; tables → chains → rules; base chains attach to hooks (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting) with a policy (accept/drop)
Default-deny = chain policy drop + explicit accept rules; stateful rule 'ct state established,related accept'
DROP vs REJECT: drop is silent (client times out), reject sends an error (client fails fast)
Docker manipulates iptables/nftables itself; rules for containers must go in the DOCKER-USER chain; published ports bypass ufw-style INPUT rules (Docker docs wording)

--network none: container has only a loopback interface; docker network create --internal creates a network with no external connectivity; default bridge docker0, containers NATed (masquerade) to the host's address; inter-container communication (icc) on default bridge is enabled by default
Containers on the same bridge network can reach each other and typically the host's bridge gateway address (host services bound to 0.0.0.0) — verify wording; host.docker.internal on Docker Desktop

sources.title: tcpdump(1), ping(8), traceroute(8), nc (ncat/openbsd netcat)
planned_claims: tcpdump -i IF -n, filter expressions (host, port, tcp/udp); needs CAP_NET_RAW/root
ping uses ICMP ECHO_REQUEST; ICMP blocked ≠ host down; ping needing CAP_NET_RAW or ping_group_range (unprivileged ICMP sockets)
traceroute uses increasing TTL and ICMP time exceeded

sources.title: Docker docs: docker container run reference; running containers
planned_claims: Flags and exact semantics: --rm, -it, -d, --name, -e/--env-file, -u/--user, -w, -v/--mount (type=bind,readonly), --read-only, --tmpfs, --network, --memory, --cpus, --pids-limit, --cap-drop/--cap-add, --security-opt no-new-privileges, --privileged, --init, --entrypoint, --ulimit
Docker exit codes: 125 docker daemon/run error, 126 contained command cannot be invoked, 127 contained command not found, otherwise the contained command's exit code
docker exec runs a new process in a running container's namespaces; -u, -w, -e flags; exec'd processes are not restarted with the container; exec default user = container's user
--privileged gives all capabilities, lifts device cgroup limits, disables seccomp/AppArmor confinement — exact doc wording

sources.title: Docker Engine security; rootless mode; userns-remap; protect the Docker daemon socket
planned_claims: Four major security areas Docker docs list: intrinsic kernel security (namespaces, cgroups), daemon attack surface, container config loopholes, kernel hardening features

Daemon requires root (unless rootless) → 'only trusted users should be allowed to control your Docker daemon'; access to the socket/docker group is root-equivalent on the host (exact wording; the bind-mount-/ example in the docs)

Default capability set: Docker starts containers with a restricted set — list exactly which capabilities are retained by default (from run reference or moby source defaults: CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FSETID, FOWNER, MKNOD, NET_RAW, SETGID, SETUID, SETFCAP, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, SYS_CHROOT, KILL, AUDIT_WRITE) — verify list and count against current docs
By default, root in a container is the SAME uid 0 as root on the host unless userns-remap/rootless is used
Rootless mode runs daemon and containers inside a user namespace as a non-root user; limitations list

sources.title: Dockerfile reference; Building best practices; build secrets; multi-stage; image digests
planned_claims: Instructions FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD, WORKDIR, ENV, ARG, USER, ENTRYPOINT vs CMD (exec vs shell form; shell form runs under /bin/sh -c so the app is not PID 1 / does not receive signals), HEALTHCHECK, STOPSIGNAL

Each RUN/COPY/ADD creates a layer; build cache invalidation rules; `apt-get update && apt-get install` must be in the same RUN (cache-busting rationale, exact doc wording); version pinning recommendation
Pin base image by digest (FROM image@sha256:…) for reproducibility: tags are mutable, digests immutable (exact wording)
ARG and ENV values persist in image metadata/history → don't use them for secrets; use --mount=type=secret; docker history / docker inspect reveal them
USER instruction: if not set, the default user is root; best-practice text about running as non-root
Multi-stage builds copy only artifacts into the final image — a way to keep build-time material (incl. reference solutions/tests) out of the task image

sources.title: Docker storage: volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs mounts
planned_claims: Volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs mounts: definitions, lifecycle (volumes persist after container removal; anonymous volumes and --rm)

Bind mounts are read-write by default: container processes can modify the HOST filesystem (docs' warning wording); readonly / :ro option; bind mount obscures existing container contents at the mount point
tmpfs mounts: memory only, not shared between containers, Linux only; size option

sources.title: Compose file reference (services, networks)
planned_claims: Service keys: image, build, command, init, user, read_only, cap_drop, security_opt, network_mode: none, networks, mem_limit / deploy.resources.limits, cpus, pids_limit, tmpfs, volumes (read_only), environment, healthcheck, depends_on
By default Compose creates one network for the app; every service joins and is reachable by service name
networks: internal: true creates an externally isolated network

sources.title: Docker logging & inspect
planned_claims: docker logs shows the container's STDOUT and STDERR (of PID 1's process tree writing to those streams); default logging driver json-file; no log rotation by default with json-file (disk-fill risk) — exact wording

docker inspect exposes Config.Env (environment variables, incl. any secrets passed with -e), Mounts, HostConfig (Memory, CapDrop, ReadonlyRootfs, NetworkMode, Privileged), State.ExitCode, State.OOMKilled

sources.title: Debian apt-get(8), apt(8), dpkg(1), dpkg-query(1), apt_preferences(5), sources.list(5); snapshot.debian.org; snapshot.ubuntu.com
planned_claims: apt-get update resynchronizes package index files from sources; install pkg=version pins a version; apt is the interactive front-end whose CLI 'may change' — scripts should use apt-get (exact wording from apt(8))
-y, --no-install-recommends, DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive (debconf(7)) to avoid interactive prompts hanging a build/agent

dpkg -l lists installed packages and versions; dpkg -S path finds owning package; dpkg -L lists files; /var/lib/dpkg/status; dpkg lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend) — the 'Could not get lock' error when two apt processes run

sources.title: gVisor documentation: What is gVisor, architecture guide, security model, performance guide
planned_claims: gVisor is an application kernel, written in Go (memory-safe), implementing a substantial portion of the Linux system call interface in userspace; runsc is its OCI runtime (drop-in for runc with Docker/Kubernetes)
Sentry intercepts application syscalls so the app never talks to the host kernel directly; Gofer mediates filesystem access; the Sentry itself uses a restricted set of host syscalls under seccomp
Trade-offs: syscall-heavy and I/O-heavy workloads pay overhead; not every syscall/feature is implemented (compatibility)
Security model statement: defends against kernel exploits via the syscall surface; what it does NOT protect against (e.g. hardware side channels, network-level policy is still yours)

sources.title: Firecracker: NSDI'20 paper (Agache et al.), firecracker-microvm.github.io, design.md, snapshot docs, jailer docs
planned_claims: Firecracker is a VMM using KVM to create microVMs; minimal device model (virtio-net, virtio-block, serial, minimal keyboard controller; no BIOS/PCI in classic design); written in Rust; powers AWS Lambda and Fargate
Headline numbers: boots to user space in ≤125 ms; <5 MiB memory overhead per microVM; creation rate up to 150 microVMs/sec/host — verify each against site and paper

Paper's argument: containers share the host kernel and rely on syscall filtering trade-offs (compatibility vs security); VMs give stronger isolation with a narrow interface; Firecracker aims for both isolation and low overhead — exact quotes from §2
Jailer: defence in depth — the VMM process itself is chrooted, namespaced, cgroup'd, seccomp-filtered, runs unprivileged

Snapshots capture full guest memory + device state; docs WARN that resuming the same snapshot multiple times duplicates state that must be unique (entropy/RNG state, identifiers, tokens), and that secrets in guest memory are in the snapshot file — exact wording
Each microVM has its own guest kernel → a guest kernel exploit does not directly give the host; the attack surface is KVM + the VMM's small device model

sources.title: Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor docs (brief context only)

sources.title: KVM kernel documentation / linux-kvm.org
planned_claims: KVM is a Linux kernel module that turns Linux into a hypervisor using hardware virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x / AMD-V; ARM virt extensions); exposed as /dev/kvm; userspace VMM (QEMU, Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor) drives it
Nested virtualization is needed to use KVM inside a cloud VM; bare metal hosts expose it directly (supports: why microVM sandboxes usually need bare metal or nested-virt instances)
